question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}$ for $s>4.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{4t}+5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{4t}\}+L\{5{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}\} \\  & =L\{{e}^{4t}\}+5L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}\}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{n}\} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{3}\} & =\frac{6}{{s}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L\{f(t)\}=F(s),$ then $L\{{e}^{at}f(t)\}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}\} & =\frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{f(t)\} & =L\{{e}^{4t}\}+5L\{{t}^{3}{e}^{-t}\} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+5\cdot \frac{6}{(s+1)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s-4}+\frac{30}{(s+1)^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>4.$
